summary: Root cause (confidence 0.85, high): the cfg-3120 feature-flag ramp on pricing-engine (flags.pricing.greeks_v2.rollout_pct 5 -> 100) at 2026-05-20T12:04:00Z put the CPU-heavy Greeks v2 Monte-Carlo path (20000 paths) on all quote traffic, driving pricing-engine CPU from ~40% to ~99% and per-request latency from ~60ms to ~2.6s, which exceeded order-service's 2500ms quote-call deadline and produced the order-service quote timeouts. The mechanism is a pure per-request CPU-cost step: pricing-engine request_rate is flat across the onset (625.14 req/s at the 12:04Z bucket vs 667.24 at 12:02Z) while cpu_pct jumps 40%->99% in the same bucket, refuting the organic-volume/capacity alternative (H4). The reporter's suspected market-data-service protobuf deploy (dep-6111, 11:56Z) is refuted: it precedes onset by 8 minutes, market-data-service shows no telemetry anomaly, and order-service's errors are timeouts, not serialization errors. The shared redis-cache/exchange-gateway degradation hypothesis is positively contradicted by flat cache CPU/clients/hit-ratio/evictions and flat exchange-gateway latency with zero component errors.

ranked_hypotheses.title: Greeks v2 rollout flag ramp to 100% saturates pricing-engine CPU, stalling quote computation
ranked_hypotheses.statement: pricing-engine's GreeksV2 calculator (Monte-Carlo, 20000 paths) is CPU-heavy. Config change cfg-3120 ramped flags.pricing.greeks_v2.rollout_pct from 5 to 100 at 12:04:00Z, putting the expensive path on all quote traffic. pricing-engine CPU jumped from ~40% to ~99% at exactly the same 12:04Z bucket with request_rate flat — a pure per-request cost step. Per-request latency rose to ~2.6s, exceeding order-service's 2500ms quote-call deadline, producing order-service quote timeouts. Origin is a feature-flag ramp (config_change); no service code shipped in this window.

causal_chain.claim: cfg-3120 ramps flags.pricing.greeks_v2.rollout_pct from 5 to 100 on pricing-engine at 12:04:00Z

Heavy GreeksV2 Monte-Carlo (20000 paths) path now exercised for all quote requests, driving pricing-engine CPU from ~40% to ~99% while memory stays flat (not memory/GC) and request_rate stays flat (not volume)
CPU saturation raises pricing-engine per-request latency to ~2.6s p99 in the same 12:04Z bucket as the CPU jump
pricing-engine's own first WARN cites 'GreeksV2Calculator: Monte-Carlo paths=20000 took ~3000-8900ms' and its own errors are GreeksV2 deadline-exceeded
order-service's http call to pricing-engine exceeds its 2500ms deadline, producing the identical 'pricing-engine quote call timed out after 2500ms' errors
Reported symptom: order-service quote timeouts at ~8% error rate from 12:04Z onward

assumptions: The flag ramp actually enabled/expanded the heavy 20000-path Monte-Carlo path (flag→CPU-cost link is inferred from timing plus F2's GreeksV2 warnings, not from direct code inspection)
The flag took effect within the 12:04–12:05 bucket (sub-minute ordering flag-apply vs CPU jump unproven, both in same 480s bucket)

ranked_hypotheses.title: Shared redis-cache / exchange-gateway degradation on the shared quote path
ranked_hypotheses.statement: A shared component (redis-cache, shared by pricing-engine and market-data-service; or exchange-gateway) degraded in the 12:04Z bucket, inflating pricing-engine latency and cascading to order-service quote timeouts.

causal_chain.claim: A shared dependency (redis-cache or exchange-gateway) begins failing/latency-spiking at onset
pricing-engine calls block on the shared dependency, raising request latency

assumptions: The shared dependency degraded without any recorded change
pricing-engine latency is dominated by the shared dependency rather than its own CPU
ranked_hypotheses.rejection_reason: Shared components were positively cleared: redis-cache CPU flat 20.4–24.13% with no step at onset (F25), connected_clients 283–349 with no step (F26), hit_ratio 93.8–98.5% and evictions 0.78–4.81 bucketed identically pre/post onset (F27), and zero ERROR logs (F29). exchange-gateway latency_p99 flat 117.5–142.6ms with no step (F28) and only one unrelated clock-drift WARN (F29). Crucially, pricing-engine's latency is CPU-bound with flat memory and flat request rate (F4, F21, F23) — an I/O-blocking shared dependency would not raise its own CPU to 99% while volume is flat.

ranked_hypotheses.title: market-data-service protobuf serialization change (reporter's suspicion) broke/slowed the quote path
ranked_hypotheses.statement: dep-6111 (market-data-service v5.2.0, 'Switch quote serialization to protobuf', 11:56:00Z) introduced new serialization that pricing-engine mis-handles, inflating quote computation time and cascading into order-service timeouts.

causal_chain.claim: dep-6111 ships protobuf quote serialization at 11:56:00Z
pricing-engine deserialization of new format is slow/buggy, inflating quote latency

assumptions: Assumed pricing-engine incurs serialization cost not visible in its logs
ranked_hypotheses.rejection_reason: dep-6111 precedes onset by 8 minutes with no market-data-service latency/error anomaly (F6, F15); order-service errors are timeouts, not serialization errors (F1); pricing-engine's own error is a GreeksV2 deadline exceeded, not a serialization error (F2); pricing-engine latency is CPU saturation, not I/O or serialization (F4).

ranked_hypotheses.title: Capacity saturation: market-open/volume-driven load exceeding pricing-engine provisioned capacity
ranked_hypotheses.statement: pricing-engine CPU saturation reflects organic quote volume growth (market open) exceeding provisioned capacity, matching historical precedent HIST-113, with order-service timeouts as a downstream symptom. No faulty change required.

causal_chain.claim: Quote traffic volume rises past pricing-engine provisioned CPU capacity at 12:04Z
pricing-engine CPU saturates and latency rises to ~2.6s

assumptions: None retained: the required volume spike does not exist in the data
ranked_hypotheses.rejection_reason: The decisive discriminator was measured and refutes it: pricing-engine request_rate is flat across 11:50–13:59Z with no step at 12:04Z (F20: 180s buckets 582–741 req/s, mean 646; the 12:04Z bucket 625.14 is BELOW the preceding 12:02Z 667.24) while CPU jumped 38–41%→~99% in the same bucket (F21). order-service request_rate is likewise flat (F22: 12:02Z 239.82 vs 12:05Z 231.73). A CPU step with no volume step is a code-path cost increase, not organic load; its only support (HIST-113 symptom match, F18) is weak precedent and HIST-113 attributes saturation to market-open volume, absent here.

facts.statement: All 225 order-service errors in the window carry one identical signature, 'pricing-engine quote call timed out after 2500ms', with no 5xx or serialization errors; the first is at 12:06:10Z — so the failing edge is order-service -> pricing-engine.

pricing-engine's earliest in-window signal is 12:05:21Z: 342 WARN 'GreeksV2Calculator: Monte-Carlo paths=20000 took ~3000-8900ms', and its first ERROR at 12:06:41Z is 'request deadline exceeded computing quote (2000ms budget) calculator=GreeksV2' — its own errors are GreeksV2 deadline-exceeded, not serialization errors.

pricing-engine latency_p99_ms jumped in the same 12:04Z bucket as order-service: ~59-61ms baseline through 11:56Z, 2291ms at 12:04Z, then ~2560-2706ms (max 2849ms); order-service latency_p99 jumped in the same bucket from ~149-154ms to 2149ms then ~2877ms, matching the reported ~2.6s.

pricing-engine latency is CPU-driven, not memory/GC-driven: cpu_pct sat ~39-41% through 11:56Z, jumped to 91.5% (max 100.0%) at 12:04Z and held ~98.7-99.3% thereafter, while memory_pct stayed flat at ~47.7-51.0% with no rise at onset.
order-service error_rate shows the same onset: flat ~0.17-0.25% through 11:56Z, then 6.08% at 12:04Z and ~8.1-8.4% thereafter (max 8.87%).

market-data-service, the service the report blames, shows no error/latency anomaly in logs in 11:00-12:20Z: only one unrelated WARN ('deprecated TLS cipher offered by client', 11:43:53Z) and zero ERROR entries.
Exactly one deployment occurred across all services in 11:00-14:00Z: dep-6111 market-data-service v5.2.0 at 11:56:00Z ('Switch quote serialization to protobuf'), status live, rolled_back_at null.

Exactly one config/flag change occurred in the window: cfg-3120 on pricing-engine, key flags.pricing.greeks_v2.rollout_pct, 5 -> 100, changed_at 2026-05-20T12:04:00Z, author pm-experiments ('Ramp Greeks v2 experiment to all traffic').
The change list is complete for the onset window: narrow re-queries of 11:40-12:20Z and 11:50-12:10Z returned the same single deployment and single config change, both partial:false.

pricing-engine request_rate did not spike at onset: at 120s resolution 623.65 (11:56Z), 647.20 (12:00Z), 667.24 (12:02Z), 625.14 (12:04Z), 666.82 (12:06Z) req/s — the onset bucket is below the preceding bucket and within baseline noise.
pricing-engine request_rate is flat across 11:50-13:59Z: 180s buckets range 582.43-741.12 req/s, mean 646.11, with no step at 12:04Z; post-onset level equals pre-onset level.

In the same 12:04Z bucket where pricing-engine request_rate was flat (625.14 req/s), cpu_pct jumped from a 38-41% baseline to avg 68.44 / max 98.65, then 98.67-99.56 for the rest of the window — a pure CPU-cost step with no request-volume change.
order-service request_rate is likewise flat with no step at 12:04Z (12:02Z avg 239.82 vs 12:05Z avg 231.73; overall range 216.83-256.97 req/s, mean 233.06).

On the quote path order-service -> pricing-engine (http) -> market-data-service (http), cfg-3120 sits on pricing-engine's quote/Greeks computation, while dep-6111 sits one hop further downstream and only affects the pricing-engine -> market-data-service edge.
redis-cache CPU is flat and low across 11:50-13:59Z with no deviation at onset (mean 21.98%, min 20.4%, max 24.13%; 12:02Z 22.0% vs 12:08Z 22.36%).
redis-cache connection saturation is absent: connected_clients stayed 283.29-348.57 (mean 311.89) with no step at onset.
redis-cache hit ratio and evictions show no degradation at onset: hit_ratio_pct 93.83-98.46% (mean 96.05), evictions_per_min 0.78-4.81 (mean 2.99), bucketed identically to pre-onset values.
exchange-gateway latency is flat, not degraded, across the window: latency_p99_ms 117.54-142.55ms (mean 130.43ms) with no step at 12:04Z.

No error/critical logs from either shared dependency in 11:50-13:59Z: redis-cache had exactly 1 WARN (TLS cipher, 13:28:54Z) and exchange-gateway exactly 1 WARN (clock drift 38ms, 12:54:21Z), neither at or near onset.

Quote-path topology: redis-cache is the shared component between pricing-engine and market-data-service, while order-service and market-data-service connect only via pricing-engine — there is no shared component directly between them.
No deployment occurred in the 2026-05-19T00:00Z-2026-05-20T11:00Z baseline window, and no order-service, ledger-db or kafka change appears in the 11:00-14:00Z results.
redis-cache exposes no latency_p99_ms and no error-rate metric at all, so its health can only be judged from CPU/clients/hit-ratio/evictions saturation proxies.

assumptions: The flag ramp actually enabled/expanded the heavy 20000-path Monte-Carlo GreeksV2 path; the flag->CPU-cost link is inferred from timing plus the GreeksV2 warnings (F2, F16), not from direct code inspection.
The flag took effect within the 12:04-12:05 bucket; sub-minute ordering between flag-apply and the CPU jump is unproven because both fall inside the same 480s bucket.

recommended_actions.action: Roll back config change cfg-3120 on pricing-engine: set flags.pricing.greeks_v2.rollout_pct from 100 back to 5 (its pre-12:04Z value), and confirm the apply in the config audit.
recommended_actions.rationale: cfg-3120 is the only change coinciding exactly with the 12:04Z onset bucket and it directly gates the GreeksV2 calculator that is emitting the 20000-path Monte-Carlo warnings and the deadline-exceeded errors (F8, F16, F2, F4). This is the same mitigation under any flag->CPU mechanism, so it is safe.

recommended_actions.action: Verify recovery in the 12:04Z-bucket metrics after the flag rollback: pricing-engine cpu_pct should return to ~40% and latency_p99 to ~60ms, and order-service error_rate should return from ~8% to ~0.2% with quote timeouts stopping.
recommended_actions.rationale: The onset is measurable in exactly these series (F3, F4, F5), so their return to baseline is a direct, observable confirmation that the flag was the cause rather than a coincidental correlation.

recommended_actions.action: Do not roll back dep-6111 (market-data-service v5.2.0 protobuf) as a first step; leave it live while the flag mitigation is tested.
recommended_actions.rationale: The serialization deploy precedes onset by 8 minutes, market-data-service shows no telemetry anomaly, and order-service errors are timeouts rather than serialization errors (F6, F7, F14, F15) — rolling it back would confound the flag experiment and is unsupported by the evidence.

recommended_actions.action: Before re-enabling the Greeks v2 ramp, size the 20000-path Monte-Carlo path: load-test pricing-engine quote traffic at 100% rollout to measure per-request CPU cost, and either reduce the path count, cache/precompute Greeks, or add capacity headroom so per-request latency stays comfortably under order-service's 2500ms deadline.
recommended_actions.rationale: The data shows a pure per-request CPU-cost step (request_rate flat, cpu 40%->99%; F19-F23) and the observed Monte-Carlo cost of ~3000-8900ms per calculation (F2); the fix must lower per-request cost, not add volume capacity.

recommended_actions.action: Add a staged rollout guard for flags.pricing.greeks_v2.rollout_pct: ramp in small increments with automatic rollback if pricing-engine cpu_pct exceeds a threshold (e.g. 85%) or latency_p99 exceeds a fraction of the 2500ms quote deadline, and surface the flag state on the pricing-engine dashboard.
recommended_actions.rationale: A 5 -> 100 single-step ramp put the heavy path on all traffic within one 480s bucket (F8, F16); incremental ramp with CPU/latency gating would have caught the cost step before order-service timeouts (F1, F5).

recommended_actions.action: Instrument redis-cache with latency_p99_ms and an error-rate metric, and ensure exchange-gateway error_rate/CPU metrics are queryable, so shared-dependency hypotheses can be positively tested rather than inferred from proxy metrics.
recommended_actions.rationale: Redis exposes no latency or error-rate metric at all (F24), and exchange-gateway error metrics were never retrievable (budget/gap), leaving H3 exclusions resting on CPU/clients/hit-ratio/evictions proxies and flat latency (F25-F29).

recommended_actions.action: Add an alert on the pricing-engine quote path when cpu_pct steps abruptly (e.g. >30 percentage points within one bucket) while request_rate is flat, since that pattern indicates a code-path cost change rather than organic load and preceded order-service impact.
recommended_actions.rationale: The decisive discriminator was a CPU step with flat request rate (F19, F21, F23); alerting on it would have detected the regression at 12:04Z rather than at the 12:16Z report.

data_gaps: Could not enumerate all services for error-rate/latency anomalies in 11:00-14:00Z (no service-catalog/topology lookup tool); only order-service, pricing-engine and market-data-service were checked, so the blast radius may be larger than established.

pricing-engine exposes no GC metric (only cpu_pct, error_rate, latency_p99_ms, memory_pct, request_rate, restarts), so GC pauses vs pure CPU saturation cannot be fully separated; only flat memory_pct plus CPU saturation are evidenced.

No code inspection or deployment/config data confirms mechanically that flipping the flag to 100% is what enabled/exercised the 20000-path Monte-Carlo path; the flag->CPU-cost link is a strong inference from timing plus F2/F16.
Config-audit shard 2/3 did not respond on the first query (partial:true) and only one retry was possible, so the change list for order-service/ledger-db/kafka cannot be guaranteed exhaustive.

The 12:04Z bucket is 480s wide and the config change is minuted at 12:04:00Z while pricing-engine's first WARN is 12:05:21Z, so sub-minute ordering between flag-apply and the CPU jump cannot be proven.

exchange-gateway error_rate, upstream_error_rate, cpu_pct, upstream_latency_ms, request_rate and restarts were never fetched (budget_exhausted), so its health rests on flat latency_p99 plus a clean 1-WARN log scan rather than on its error metric.
redis-cache has no latency_p99_ms or error-rate metric instrumented (latency query returned not_found), so redis slowness cannot be measured directly.
No rollback of cfg-3120 or dep-6111 is recorded in the window, so the mitigation state at the current time (13:59Z) is unknown.
what_would_change_the_conclusion: A measured request-volume spike at 12:04Z on pricing-engine or order-service (contradicting the flat request_rate in F19-F22) would point back to organic capacity/market-open saturation (H4) rather than a code-path cost increase.

Evidence that pricing-engine CPU returned to ~40% and latency to ~60ms without rolling back cfg-3120 (e.g. a spontaneous recovery or a different change taking effect) would break the flag->CPU causal link and force a re-ranking.
Finding an error/latency or serialization anomaly in market-data-service or on the pricing-engine -> market-data-service edge at 11:56-12:06Z would revive the protobuf serialization hypothesis (H2).

Evidence of redis-cache or exchange-gateway degradation at 12:04Z (e.g. redis latency/error metrics or exchange-gateway error/CPU saturation, which were never fetched) would revive the shared-component hypothesis (H3).
Logs or code showing the GreeksV2 calculator was already running at 20000 paths (or on all traffic) before 12:04Z would decouple cfg-3120 from the CPU step and undermine the top hypothesis.

Historical precedent HIST-113 (2026-01-28, pricing-engine CPU saturation at market open, symptoms 'quote timeouts','cpu 99%', root cause record market-open volume exceeding capacity) is the closest match by symptom to this incident — but it is a lead, not evidence: HIST-113 attributes the CPU saturation to market-open volume, whereas here the saturation coincides with a Greeks v2 rollout flag, not with a market-open time.

findings.statement: pricing-engine request_rate did NOT spike at the 12:04Z onset bucket: at 120s resolution it reads 623.65 (11:56Z), 606.28 (11:58Z), 647.20 (12:00Z), 667.24 (12:02Z), 625.14 (12:04Z), 666.82 (12:06Z) req/s — i.e. the 12:04Z bucket (625.14) is BELOW the preceding 12:02Z bucket (667.24) and within the baseline noise band.

pricing-engine request_rate is flat across the whole 11:50–13:59Z window: 180s buckets range only 582.43–741.12 req/s, mean 646.11, with no step at 12:04Z (12:02Z avg 653.76, 12:05Z avg 652.37, 12:08Z 634.18); the post-onset level equals the pre-onset level.

In the SAME 12:04Z bucket where pricing-engine request_rate was flat (625.14), cpu_pct jumped from a 38-41% baseline to avg 68.44 / max 98.65, then 98.67-99.56 for the rest of the window — a pure CPU-cost step with no corresponding request volume change.

order-service request_rate over the same 11:50–13:59Z window is flat and shows no step at 12:04Z: the 12:02Z bucket avg 239.82 vs the 12:05Z bucket avg 231.73, and the overall range is only 216.83–256.97 req/s (mean 233.06) — no capacity ramp on the caller side either.

Discriminator verdict: a flat request rate coinciding with a 40%→99% CPU jump confirms H1 (fixed code-path cost per request from the Greeks v2 rollout) and is inconsistent with H4 (organic volume / market-open capacity saturation), which requires a request-volume spike that is absent from both pricing-engine and order-service.

redis-cache exposes NO latency or error-rate metric at all: a query for 'latency_p99_ms' failed with not_found and the only available metrics are 'connected_clients','cpu_pct','evictions_per_min','hit_ratio_pct','memory_pct'. So redis-cache health can only be judged from saturation/proxy metrics, not from latency/errors.

redis-cache CPU is flat and low across the whole 11:50-13:59Z window, showing no deviation at 12:04Z onset: mean 21.98%, min 20.4%, max 24.13%; the 12:02Z bucket is 22.0% avg and 12:08Z is 22.36% avg, i.e. the onset bucket is indistinguishable from the 11:50Z baseline (22.31%).

redis-cache connection saturation is absent: connected_clients stayed in a narrow band with no step at onset — min 283.29, max 348.57, mean 311.89; 12:02Z avg 310.12 vs 12:08Z avg 319.2, both within the 11:50Z (314.14) / 11:56Z (311.24) baseline range.

redis-cache hit ratio and evictions show no degradation at onset: hit_ratio_pct held 93.83-98.46% (mean 96.05) with 12:02Z=96.39 and 12:08Z=96.02; evictions_per_min held 0.78-4.81 (mean 2.99) with 12:02Z=3.32 and 12:08Z=2.98 — both bucketed identically to the pre-onset 11:50-11:56Z values.

exchange-gateway latency is flat, not degraded, across the window: latency_p99_ms ranges 117.54-142.55ms with mean 130.43ms; the 12:02Z bucket is 128.87ms and 12:08Z is 133.78ms, entirely within the 11:50Z (131.94) and 11:56Z (130.49) baseline. No step at 12:04Z onset.

No error/critical log evidence from either shared dependency in 11:50-13:59Z: redis-cache returned exactly 1 WARN total ('deprecated TLS cipher offered by client 46e36f97' at 13:28:54Z) and exchange-gateway exactly 1 WARN ('clock drift 38ms detected, resyncing with NTP' at 12:54:21Z), both truncated:false and neither at or near the 12:04Z onset.
